passages.t: A light on the Damascus road
passages.happening:
Saul is “still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord” (verse 1). He asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that he can arrest any men or women “belonging to the Way” and bring them to Jerusalem as prisoners (verse 2).

Near Damascus, “suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him” (verse 3). He falls to the ground and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” (verse 4). He asks, “Who are You, Lord?” The answer comes: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (verse 5). He is told to go into the city and wait to be told what to do.

The men with him stand speechless. “They heard the voice but did not see anyone” (verse 7). Saul gets up, but he is blind. They lead him by the hand into Damascus, and for three days he neither eats nor drinks (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Damascus was an old city in Syria, about 220 kilometres (some 135 miles) north-east of Jerusalem, several days' walk. It had a large Jewish community with several synagogues. A synagogue was a local Jewish meeting place for prayer and the reading of Scripture. Some of its members had come to believe in Jesus, and Saul wanted the high priest's letters so the synagogues would hand them over.

‘The Way’ is one of the earliest names for the followers of Jesus (it comes again in 19:9, 23 and 24:14). It names a way of living, not only a set of ideas.

Notice what the voice says. Saul thinks he is hunting down a group of misled Jews. Jesus says, ‘why do you persecute Me?’ To hurt his people is to hurt him. Paul would later teach that the church is the body of Christ, and many readers think he first learned it here.

Saul set out with authority and letters. He arrives blind, led by the hand. A first hearer would feel how complete the reversal is.

Luke tells this event three times: here, in Paul's speech to the crowd in Jerusalem (22:6-16), and in his speech to King Agrippa (26:12-18). Only one other story in Acts is retold like this: Peter and Cornelius (chapters 10, 11 and 15). It is that important to Luke.
passages.ot:
The double name, ‘Saul, Saul’, is how God called his servants in the Old Testament at turning points. “Abraham, Abraham!” the angel calls on the mountain (Genesis 22:11). From the burning bush God calls, “Moses, Moses!” (Exodus 3:4). In the night the LORD calls, “Samuel! Samuel!” (1 Samuel 3:10). A first hearer who knew the Scriptures would sense that this is not only a rebuke but a call.

Paul himself describes the moment in the words of the prophets. He writes that God “set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace” (Galatians 1:15), which echoes Jeremiah, “before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5), and Isaiah's servant, “The LORD called Me from the womb” (Isaiah 49:1).

The light also points to Isaiah. God's servant would be “a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind” (Isaiah 42:6-7). Saul, who will carry that light to the nations, is first made blind himself.
passages.hard:
Luke tells the event three times, and the tellings differ in small ways. Here the men with Saul ‘heard the voice but did not see anyone’ (verse 7). In 22:9 Paul says, “My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me.” Many older Bibles translate 22:9 as ‘they heard not the voice’, which seems to say the opposite of 9:7.

Readers account for this in more than one way. Many point out that the Greek verb for ‘hear’ can mean either to hear a sound or to understand what is said, and that the two verses use different grammar. On this reading the men heard a sound but did not catch the words. That is why the Berean Standard Bible translates 22:9 ‘could not understand’. Other scholars think the difference in grammar is too slight to carry that much weight, and that Luke simply tells the story with different details each time, as ancient historians often did. The book page's list of hard passages names this question too.

There are other differences. In chapter 26 Jesus gives Saul his task on the road; here it comes through Ananias. Luke wrote all three tellings himself, in one book, and did not seem to think they clashed. All three agree on the centre: a light, a voice, Jesus naming himself as the one Saul was persecuting, and a call to carry his name to the nations.
passages.asks: Saul was sure he was serving God, and he was wrong. Ask where your own certainty might be blinding you. And notice how Jesus speaks to his enemy: not with a curse, but by name, with a question. Jesus' question to Saul is a question to anyone who hurts his people: ‘why do you persecute Me?’

passages.happening:
In Damascus there is a disciple named Ananias. The Lord speaks to him in a vision and tells him to go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for “a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying” (verse 11). Saul has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come and lay hands on him to restore his sight.

Ananias objects. “Lord, many people have told me about this man and all the harm he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem” (verse 13), and now he has come with authority to arrest them all.

The Lord answers, “Go!” and then, “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel” (verse 15). “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name” (verse 16).

So Ananias goes. He lays his hands on Saul. “Brother Saul,” he says, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit” (verse 17). Something like scales falls from Saul's eyes. He can see. He gets up and is baptized, eats, and regains his strength (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
This is a different Ananias from the man in chapter 5. In 22:12 Paul describes him as “a devout observer of the law who was highly regarded by all the Jews living there.” He was a faithful Jew who believed that Jesus was the Messiah.

Think about what he is asked to do. Saul has come to Damascus to arrest people like Ananias. Everyone in the small group of believers knows it. To walk into the house where Saul is staying, give his name, and lay hands on him, is to risk prison or worse. Ananias argues with the Lord, honestly. Then he goes.

His first words are the bravest in the chapter: ‘Brother Saul’. Before Saul has done anything to earn trust, Ananias calls him family.

Tarsus was Saul's home city, a large and well-known city in Cilicia, in the south of what is now Turkey. Straight Street was a long main street running through Damascus.

The Lord's words to Ananias set the shape of Saul's whole life. He will carry Jesus' name ‘before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel’. Gentiles are people who are not Jewish. Notice that Israel is still in the list. Saul's call is not away from his own people.

‘How much he must suffer’ is not a threat. It is honesty. Years later Paul would list his beatings, his shipwrecks, and his dangers ‘from my countrymen and from the Gentiles’ (2 Corinthians 11:26).
passages.ot:
Ananias answers the Lord the way the prophets did: “Here I am, Lord” (verse 10). Samuel said, “Speak, for Your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:10). Isaiah said, “Here am I. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). And like Moses and Jeremiah before him, Ananias first raises an objection, and is answered.

Saul is called ‘My chosen instrument’ to carry God's name to the nations. Isaiah had said of the servant of the LORD, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Later, in Acts 13:47, Paul quotes that verse about his own work.
passages.hard:
Was this a conversion or a call? Christians and scholars describe it in two ways, and both have strong support.

Some scholars say it is better called a call than a conversion. Saul did not change gods. He went on worshipping the God of Abraham, and he never stopped calling himself a Jew: “I am an Israelite myself” (Romans 11:1). When he tells the story in Galatians, he uses the language of a prophet's call (Galatians 1:15-16). On this view, the God he had always served gave him a new task.

Others reply that it is a conversion as well. Saul turned from fighting Jesus to worshipping him as Lord. He later wrote that he counted all he had been proud of as loss: “I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). On this view his life was turned around at its centre.

Many readers find both in the text: a Jew called by the God of his fathers, and a persecutor turned to the one he had persecuted. These notes leave the choice of word to the reader.
passages.asks: Ananias was afraid, and he said so. Then he went, and his first word was ‘Brother’. Ask whom you find hardest to call brother or sister, and what it would take to walk into that room. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is going anyway, when the Lord says go.

passages.t: Preaching in Damascus, and the basket
passages.happening:
Saul begins at once to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues: “He is the Son of God” (verse 20). Everyone who hears him is astonished. Isn't this the man who attacked the believers in Jerusalem and came here to take them as prisoners? (verse 21). But Saul grows stronger, and he confounds the Jews of Damascus, “proving that Jesus is the Christ” (verse 22).

“After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him” (verse 23). Saul learns of the plot. They watch the city gates day and night to kill him. “One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Saul goes straight to the synagogues, the same places where he had meant to make arrests. He argues as a Jew among Jews, from the Jewish Scriptures, that Jesus is the Christ, which means the Messiah, the King God had promised.

Then Luke writes, ‘the Jews conspired to kill him’. Read the words carefully. Luke means some people in Damascus who opposed Saul, not the Jewish people. Saul himself is a Jew. So is Ananias. So are the disciples who lower him over the wall. In the same city, Jewish believers in Jesus are hiding him. ‘The Jews’ here is a name for one group of opponents in one city, at one time. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later misused against Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

Paul tells this escape himself. He writes that in Damascus “the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp” (2 Corinthians 11:32-33). Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, an Arab kingdom east and south of Judea, from about 9 BC to AD 40. Historians debate how his officer had power in Damascus at that time. Acts names the plotters; Paul names the king's governor. Many readers think both were part of the same danger.

‘After many days’ covers more time than it sounds. In Galatians Paul says that after his call he went away into Arabia, came back to Damascus, and only after three years went up to Jerusalem (Galatians 1:17-18). Luke does not mention Arabia. The book page's part on Acts and Paul's letters sets the two side by side.
passages.ot:
Saul's message, that Jesus is ‘the Son of God’ and ‘the Christ’, comes from Israel's Scriptures. In the Psalms God says to his anointed king, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:7). Paul would later quote that verse about Jesus' rising (13:33).

The escape by night through a window in the wall has an old echo too. In Jericho, Rahab “let them down by a rope through the window” (Joshua 2:15), and the two spies escaped. And when King Saul sent men to kill David, “Michal lowered David from the window, and he ran away and escaped” (1 Samuel 19:12). The new Saul escapes the way David escaped the old one.
passages.asks: The man who came to Damascus with letters to arrest people leaves it in a basket, at night, helped by the people he came to arrest. Ask whether you are willing to be helped by those you once looked down on. And notice that Paul did not hide this undignified exit. Years later he told it himself, as a sign of weakness, not strength.

passages.happening:
When Saul arrives in Jerusalem, he tries to join the disciples, but they are all afraid of him. They do not believe he is a disciple (verse 26).

“Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles” (verse 27). He tells them how Saul saw the Lord on the road, how the Lord spoke to him, and how Saul preached boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus. So Saul stays with them and speaks boldly in Jerusalem (verse 28).

He talks and debates with the Grecian Jews, and they try to kill him (verse 29). When the believers learn of it, they take him down to Caesarea and send him off to Tarsus (verse 30).

“Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace” (verse 31). It grows in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.
passages.hearers:
The believers' fear makes sense. The last time they saw Saul, he was dragging their friends to prison. A changed story is easy to fake. They had no reason yet to trust it.

Barnabas did. We met him in 4:36: a Levite from Cyprus whose name the apostles gave him, meaning ‘son of encouragement’. Here he lives up to the name. He takes the risk of vouching for Saul when no one else will. Without Barnabas, Saul might never have been trusted by the church.

The ‘Grecian Jews’ were Greek-speaking Jews, many of them from outside the land. These were the same kind of people who had argued with Stephen (6:9). Saul had once stood with those who killed Stephen (8:1). Now he takes Stephen's place, and they try to kill him too. Again, these are some people in one group in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people; the believers who save Saul are Jews as well.

Paul's own account in Galatians says that on this visit he stayed with Peter (whom he calls Cephas) for fifteen days and saw no other apostle except James, the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:18-19). Luke's ‘apostles’ may be a general way of speaking. The book page sets out how readers fit the two accounts together.

Caesarea was the port on the coast where the Roman governors lived. From there Saul sails home to Tarsus. He will stay out of the story until Barnabas fetches him again (11:25).

Verse 31 is a summary, one of several in Acts. It marks the end of a stage. The good news has now reached ‘Judea, Galilee, and Samaria’, as Jesus had said it would (1:8).
passages.ot:
The Law said that a matter must be settled by more than one voice: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Saul's word about himself is not enough for the church. Barnabas adds his witness, and that opens the door.

‘The fear of the Lord’ is an old phrase from the Scriptures. It does not mean terror. It means reverence, a deep respect for God that shapes how a person lives. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10).
passages.asks: Every changed person needs a Barnabas: someone who will stand next to them when others are still afraid. Ask whether there is someone whose new start you could vouch for. And ask, too, whether you have been slow to believe that God can change a person you know.

passages.happening:
As Peter travels through the area, he goes to visit the saints in Lydda (verse 32). The ‘saints’ are the believers; the word means people set apart for God.

There he finds a man named Aeneas, who has been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years (verse 33). “Aeneas,” Peter says, “Jesus Christ heals you! Get up and put away your mat” (verse 34). Immediately Aeneas gets up. Everyone who lives in Lydda and Sharon sees him and turns to the Lord (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Lydda (the old town of Lod) lay north-west of Jerusalem, on the edge of the coastal plain of Sharon. There are already believers there, and Luke does not say who brought them the good news. The scattering of chapter 8 has carried the good news into the towns of the coast.

Peter's words matter: ‘Jesus Christ heals you’. Peter does not claim the power for himself. He points the man, and everyone watching, to Jesus. In 3:12 he had said the same: not our power.

Eight years in bed meant eight years of being carried, fed and washed by others. For Aeneas, being able to ‘put away your mat’ (some think it means ‘make your bed’) was a return to an ordinary life with dignity.

The story echoes Jesus' own words to a paralyzed man: ‘Get up, pick up your mat’ (Mark 2:11). What Jesus did in Galilee, he goes on doing through his people.
passages.ot:
The prophets looked for a day when God would heal his people: “Then the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). The healings in Acts are signs that this promised time has begun in Jesus.

Sharon was the coastal plain known in the Old Testament for its beauty and fertility. Isaiah says that in the day of God's renewal the desert will be given “the splendor of Carmel and Sharon” (Isaiah 35:2), and Sharon's flowers became a picture of beauty (Song of Songs 2:1).
passages.hard:
Aeneas was healed in an instant. Many who are sick or disabled today pray for healing that does not come. What does this story say to them?

The note on Acts 3:1-10 speaks to this. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul begged the Lord three times to take away his ‘thorn in the flesh’ and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He left his friend Trophimus “sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). None of these men are blamed.

And if you live with a disability or an illness that has not been healed, this story is not a judgment on your faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Peter did not say, ‘I heal you’. He said, ‘Jesus Christ heals you’. Ask whether the good you do points people to yourself or to him. And remember the eight years. Some waits are long, and God has not forgotten the people in them.

passages.happening:
In Joppa there is a disciple named Tabitha, also called Dorcas, who is “always occupied with works of kindness and charity” (verse 36). She becomes sick and dies. Her body is washed and laid in an upper room (verse 37).

The disciples hear that Peter is in Lydda, nearby, and send two men to urge him, “Come to us without delay” (verse 38). When he arrives, they take him upstairs. “All the widows stood around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them” (verse 39).

Peter sends them all out of the room. He kneels and prays. Then, turning to the body, he says, “Tabitha, get up!” She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up (verse 40). He takes her by the hand, helps her up, and presents her alive to the saints and the widows (verse 41).

The news spreads all over Joppa, and many believe in the Lord (verse 42). Peter stays there for some days with a tanner named Simon (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Joppa (modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv) was a port on the coast, about 18 kilometres (11 miles) from Lydda. Tabitha is an Aramaic name and Dorcas a Greek one. Both mean ‘gazelle’. Luke gives both, as if the church there used both languages.

She is called ‘a disciple’. Luke uses the feminine form of the Greek word, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Her life is told through what she made. The widows show Peter the clothes she sewed for them. In that world a widow often had no one to provide for her. Tabitha had clothed them with her own hands. Their grief is also fear: who will care for them now?

Washing the body and laying it out was the loving work of family and friends before burial.

Notice how closely Peter follows Jesus. When Jesus raised the daughter of Jairus, he sent the mourners out, took the girl by the hand and said, “Talitha koum!” (Mark 5:41), which means ‘Little girl, get up’. Peter sends everyone out, kneels and prays, and says, ‘Tabitha, get up’. If Peter spoke Aramaic here, as many think, his words would have been ‘Tabitha koum’, one letter different from ‘Talitha koum’. Peter had been in that room with Jesus (Mark 5:37). He does what he saw his Lord do, but first he kneels and prays, because the power is not his.

Then a small detail: Peter stays with ‘a tanner named Simon’. Tanners made leather from the skins of dead animals, and the work smelled foul. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, lists a tanner among the men whose wives could ask a court to make them grant a divorce (Mishnah Ketubot 7:10), it seems because of the smell. Many readers also think a tanner was counted ritually unclean, because he handled dead bodies of animals; others argue the rabbis objected to the smell and the dirt, not to uncleanness. Either way, Peter is lodging in a house many would avoid, and the next chapter will push him much further.
passages.ot:
Peter's prayer in a closed upper room recalls the two great prophets. Elijah carried a widow's dead son “to the upper room where he was staying” and cried out to the LORD, and “the child’s life returned to him” (1 Kings 17:19, 22). Elisha went into the room where a boy lay dead, “closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD” (2 Kings 4:33). In both stories the child is given back to a mother. Here a woman is given back to the widows who depended on her.

Joppa itself has an Old Testament story. It was the port where the prophet Jonah boarded a ship to run away from God's call to a foreign city (Jonah 1:3). The next chapter begins in Joppa too, and there Peter will be sent, against his own instincts, to a foreigner.
passages.hard:
Tabitha was raised, and the widows had her back. Many have prayed beside the bed of someone they loved, as these friends did, and the person did not wake. What does this story say to them?

It does not say that their prayers were too weak, or that God loved Tabitha more. Luke tells only a few such stories, and they are signs, not promises that every death will be undone now. Tabitha herself would one day die again, as Lazarus did. The signs point forward to a day that is still coming, when God “will wipe away every tear” (Revelation 21:4).

If you have lost someone, grief is not a lack of faith. The widows in this room wept openly, and no one told them to stop. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Tabitha is remembered by what she made for others: tunics and clothing for women who had no one else. Ask what your hands are making that someone will hold up and show, one day, when they speak of you. Small, faithful kindness is not small to God.
